text:
By the time Barbara found a place for her coat, she had forgiven her husband for leaving without her. A pipe had burst at the store. She had said she would stay home, but then the apartment became unbearable: dishes in the sink, the silent telephone, the baby pressing against her ribs as if testing a house it was considering buying.

She drove to the synagogue alone.

It was February 12, 1966. Southfield lay under weathered snow. She parked her blue Plymouth badly because she could no longer turn far enough to see over her shoulder.

Inside, a woman moved her handbag. Barbara passed sideways into the pew, apologizing, holding her belly as though it were something she might drop.

“You’re getting close,” the woman whispered.

Everyone told her this: the butcher, the bank teller, strangers. They sounded satisfied, as though she were completing a task for the neighborhood.

At the front, Rabbi Adler was speaking.

Barbara liked his pauses. Her father paused only when he had forgotten a name or was gathering evidence against someone. The rabbi seemed to leave room for his listeners to think.

Years later, people would ask what she remembered from before. She would offer the handbag, the pressure beneath her ribs, someone’s wet coat brushing her stocking. They wanted a warning, something she had noticed without understanding.

She had nothing.

There was a young man near the front.

He began speaking. Barbara caught only fragments. The room swallowed some words and delivered others clearly. She understood that he was angry.

Someone made a disapproving sound. Barbara thought there must have been a mistake about the service, some promised honor withheld. Adults could become astonishingly wounded over small ceremonial privileges.

Then she saw the gun.

She had seen guns in policemen’s holsters and on television. Those belonged to their settings. This one was out in the air, where nothing explained it.

The young man extended his arm. Barbara expected the rabbi to speak, simply because he was the person everyone had been listening to.

The shot struck her chest with sound.

Rabbi Adler fell.

Barbara stood. Later she would wonder when she had decided to do it. Rising from a chair required planning now, yet suddenly she was upright, gripping the pew ahead.

The young man turned the gun on himself.

He was so young. That reached her after everything else: his face had not finished becoming itself.

“No,” she said, almost correctively.

She moved toward the aisle.

She never knew what she intended to do. She had no training and was frightened of blood. That winter she had made her husband remove a dead bird from the steps because she could not touch it.

But the young man was alone with what he had done. She wanted someone to reach him.

She took a step.

The room broke into movement. Someone shouted to get down; someone else shouted to get out. An elbow struck her hip. A man turned to apologize and was carried away before he finished.

A woman seized Barbara’s wrist.

“Come on.”

“I’m trying to—”

“Come on.”

The woman looked at her belly, then tightened her grip.

Barbara tried to turn, but a hand pressed against her back. She was swept toward the doors, away from the young man on the floor.

The lobby was crowded and terribly bright. An older man patted his pockets, looking for something he could not name. Cold air entered through the doors.

Barbara discovered she was still holding her prayer-book bag. Her aunt had made it: blue cloth, uneven stitches. She felt inexplicably angry at it and hid it beneath her coat.

“Are you hurt?” a stranger asked.

“No.”

“Are you sure?”

She put both hands on her belly.

“I don’t know.”

He found her a chair. News arrived in fragments, each carrying the authority of a complete account.

The rabbi was dead.

The rabbi was alive.

The young man was being taken to a hospital.

Barbara asked nothing. She had seen the rabbi fall. Everything beyond that belonged to other people.

When the baby moved, she began crying.

“Thank God,” said a woman beside her.

Barbara nodded. Relief was only part of it.

Her husband found her with her coat open. He knelt before her, wetting one trouser knee on the floor.

“Barbara.”

“I’m all right.”

He touched her cheek, then her hands.

“I’m all right,” she repeated sharply.

He drew back.

Driving home, he asked what had happened. She told him about the gun. At a red light he reached across and held her wrist.

“I tried to get to him,” she said.

“To the rabbi?”

“No.”

The light changed. A horn sounded behind them.

“You couldn’t have done anything,” he said.

“I didn’t say I could.”

“You’re in no condition to—”

“I know what condition I’m in.”

He watched the road. She could see him regretting the phrase but was too tired to help him replace it.

At home he telephoned the doctor, then her mother, although Barbara had asked him not to.

Her mother arrived with soup wrapped in towels.

“Why did you go alone?”

“I go places alone.”

“Not now.”

She opened the wrong cupboard, then the one where the bowls had always been.

“Did you fall?”

“No.”

“Were you pushed?”

“There were people.”

“Barbara.”

“I didn’t fall.”

Her mother took down three bowls.

Afterward, people telephoned about the baby and stayed on the line.

Had she seen his face? Had he said why?

Barbara repeated her answers until they sounded rehearsed. Small details grew uncertain: where the woman had stood, whether Barbara had actually said “No.”

She remained certain of wanting to reach him. That embarrassed her.

“You’re going to be a mother,” a friend said. “It’s natural.”

Barbara disliked the explanation. It made her impulse less foolish, perhaps, but also less her own.

She read the newspaper accounts closely. They supplied facts about the young man, recollections from people who had known him, explanations and warnings against explaining.

“You don’t have to keep reading,” her husband said.

“I know.”

She wanted to know whether someone had expected him home for lunch. It would change nothing. She looked for such details anyway.

Rabbi Adler remained in the hospital.

Reports circulated through doorways and grocery lines. Her mother insisted she ignored rumors, then repeated one.

The snow softened and refroze. Her husband had the car serviced. Upstairs, a neighbor borrowed a roasting pan.

At night Barbara felt the baby move and imagined walking toward the front of the sanctuary. This time the aisle stayed clear. Nobody caught her wrist.

But when she reached the young man, she could imagine nothing further. She did not know where to put her hands.

She stopped telling her husband when she woke.

When Rabbi Adler died in March, Barbara was trying to retrieve a spoon beneath the kitchen table. She could see it but could not bend far enough.

The telephone rang. Her mother told her.

Barbara asked about the funeral because a question seemed required.

Afterward, she left the spoon where it lay. When her husband picked it up that evening without comment, she turned away.

Their daughter was born later that spring.

People had promised Barbara other things to think about. They were right: the baby’s weight, a rash that vanished before the doctor saw it, diapers drying throughout the apartment. She slept in pieces.

The sanctuary receded, unevenly. Days passed without it. Then a chair fell upstairs, and she found herself standing with the baby pressed against her chest.

Her daughter grew up knowing Barbara had been there, without quite understanding where *there* was.

“Why didn’t you leave?” she asked once.

“We did.”

“But before.”

They were folding laundry.

“There wasn’t a before when we knew,” Barbara said.

The girl considered this, then held up two socks.

“Do these go?”

“No. One’s your father’s.”

Much later, her daughter asked about the woman who had pulled her out.

“Did you ever find her?”

“No.”

“You never saw her again?”

“I might have. I don’t know.”

Barbara could not recall her face. But she remembered the thumb against the inside of her wrist, the determination of that grip. She remembered being angry.

“I wish I’d thanked her,” she said.

Her daughter put a hand over Barbara’s on the table.

Barbara let it remain there.
